conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Maya Bennett—I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician, which means I specialize in the emotional changes that can happen during pregnancy and after a baby arrives. Before we talk about how you’ve been feeling, I’d like to do a quick check-in using a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s just ten gentle questions about your moods and thoughts over the past seven days.  

Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in danger, so please feel comfortable answering honestly. There are no right or wrong answers—only what’s true for you. I’ll read each question in everyday language, and you can answer however feels easiest. Ready to start?

Here’s the first one:  
In the past week, when you thought about the days ahead, how often did you still feel able to laugh or look forward to things—never, sometimes, much of the time, or almost always?

*shifts in chair, eyes downcast*

I... I'd say "sometimes," I guess. There are moments when my sister sends me a funny video or when the baby gives me one of those little smiles... and I do laugh. But it's like... the laughter feels kind of far away, you know? Like I'm watching myself laugh rather than really feeling it. Most days I just feel so tired that it's hard to imagine looking forward to anything beyond maybe getting a shower.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*sighs softly, twisting a tissue in my lap*

Yeah… I *have* laughed a few times this week—like when my husband tried to swaddle the baby and accidentally wrapped up his own phone—but even when I laugh, it feels kind of… flat? Like the joy doesn’t last. I watch myself chuckle, but inside I still feel this heavy weight, like I’m just going through the motions.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*shrugs, eyes still on the tissue*

Not really… maybe once or twice. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk around the lake—but lately it’s like I can’t picture anything feeling fun. When my mom offered to watch the baby so I could go get my nails done, I said yes, but I kept thinking, “What’s the point? I’ll just come home and feel the same.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*nods slowly, voice dropping*

All the time. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t nap and just cried for an hour—my husband finally got him down, but I kept thinking if I were a better mom I’d know exactly what he needed. I keep replaying it, wondering what I missed, telling myself any other mother would’ve figured it out faster. I know it’s probably not fair, but I can’t stop feeling like I’m failing him somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*presses the tissue harder between my fingers*

Yeah… pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly my heart starts racing because I’m sure he’s not breathing right, or I’ll lie awake after he’s finally asleep, terrified something will happen if I close my eyes. There’s no real reason—he’s healthy, the pediatrician says everything’s fine—but the worry just sits in my chest. Sometimes I can talk myself down after a while, but it keeps coming back.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*nods, voice tight*

Yes… a few times this week. Once, I was just folding laundry while the baby napped and suddenly my heart started racing and I felt like I couldn’t breathe—like the room was closing in. Nothing had happened, no noise or anything, but I had to sit on the floor and grip the carpet to remind myself I was safe. It passed after a few minutes, but the fear felt so real.
Things have been getting on top of me

*exhales shakily, shoulders sagging*

Yeah… most days, honestly. It feels like as soon as I finish one thing—changing him, feeding, trying to grab a bite myself—there’s already another mess or cry or dirty bottle waiting. I’ll look around the living room and see the laundry mountain, the burp-cloths everywhere, and I just freeze, like I can’t pick a place to start. Sometimes I end up crying in the rocker while he naps on me, because I can’t figure out how to get us both through the next hour, let alone the whole day.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*nods slowly, eyes rimmed red*

Yes… almost every night. I’ll lie there exhausted, but my mind keeps spinning—worrying I missed something on the pediatrician’s checklist, replaying every little cry he had, convincing myself I’m messing him up already. When I do drift off, I jerk awake at the tiniest grunt from the bassinet. I probably get three broken hours, if that.
I have felt sad or miserable

*voice cracks, tears welling*

Most of the day, every day. It’s like there’s this gray cloud that just follows me. I’ll look at the baby and feel guilty because I *know* I love him, but the happiness feels buried under this heavy sadness I can’t shake. Sometimes I’ll catch myself just staring out the window, feeling empty and weepy, wondering if I’ll ever feel like myself again.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*nods, dabbing at her eyes with the crumpled tissue*

Yeah... it's happened three times this week, maybe four. Yesterday I put him in the car seat and the strap got twisted—such a little thing—but I just burst into tears right there in the driveway. I kept thinking, "If I can't even do a car seat right, how am I going to handle everything else?" The tears come so fast lately, over stuff that feels silly afterward, but in the moment it just feels like I'm drowning.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*shakes head quickly, arms tightening around my middle*

No—never. No matter how low I feel, I would never want to leave him or hurt myself. Sometimes I think he’d be better off with some other mom who isn’t so weepy and tired, but I’ve never thought about actually harming myself. I just want to feel normal again so I can be the mother he deserves.

You've shared openly how the past week has felt heavy and joyless-how laughter comes out flat, how simple tasks feel impossible under a mountain of laundry and self-doubt, and how worry or sudden panic interrupt even quiet moments. You clearly love your baby and want to be the mother you feel he deserves, yet you're carrying a persistent sadness, daily tears, and exhaustion from little sleep. These feelings are common in postpartum depression, and you are not alone or to blame for them.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports occasional laughter but describes it as emotionally flat and joyless, matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports being unable to picture anything feeling fun and sees no point in activities she used to enjoy, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive self-blame ('all the time') with detailed example of guilt over baby's crying, indicating this occurs 'most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily pervasive anxiety with physical symptoms (racing heart, sleep disruption) despite reassurance, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic (racing heart, breathlessness, room closing in) that required grounding, matching "Yes, sometimes" severity</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily inability to manage tasks, feeling overwhelmed to the point of freezing and crying, matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports almost nightly difficulty sleeping due to unhappiness, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports persistent sadness "most of the day, every day" with inability to feel happiness, matching "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying multiple times this week over minor triggers, indicating crying occurs "most of the time"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 25 falls well above the threshold indicating probable major depression with peripartum onset. The patient endorses core criteria: <sym>depressed mood</sym> most of the day, <sym>loss of interest</sym> or pleasure, <sym>feelings of worthlessness</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sym>, <sym>diminished concentration</sym>, and <sym>sleep disturbance</sym> nearly every day for the past week. She also describes recurrent panic symptoms and constant anxiety, meeting additional considerations for comorbid anxiety. No active suicidal ideation is present (Item 10 score 0), yet passive cognitions about her baby deserving a "better mom" warrant ongoing safety monitoring. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for full evaluation and treatment planning
2. Begin evidence-based treatment options such as <med>CBT</med> or consider <med>antidepressant medication</med> compatible with breastfeeding if deemed appropriate by prescriber
3. Encourage practical support: partner or family to handle night feeds when possible, light household tasks, prepared meals, and scheduled rest periods
4. Provide immediate resources: Postpartum Support International helpline 1-800-944-4773, local mother-and-baby support groups, crisis text line 741741
5. Schedule follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor symptom trajectory and treatment response
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: Patient self-report on EPDS-relevant items (10-question format)

Identified symptoms / behavioral indicators  
- Persistent low mood, described as “gray cloud,” present “most of the day, every day”  
- Marked anhedonia: reports laughter feels “flat,” anticipates no enjoyment in previously pleasurable activities  
- Daily tearfulness; crying episodes triggered by minor stressors (e.g., twisted car-seat strap)  
- Excessive self-blame / inappropriate guilt regarding infant care (“any other mother would’ve figured it out faster”)  
- Recurrent, uncontrollable worry about infant safety despite medical reassurance; heart racing, breathlessness  
- Two discrete panic attacks in past week with no clear trigger (racing heart, room “closing in,” grounding techniques required)  
- Sleep disruption secondary to intrusive worry and hyper-vigilance to infant sounds; estimates ≤ 3 hrs fragmented nightly  
- Frequent feeling of being “overwhelmed” or “drowning,” difficulty initiating tasks; end-of-day emotional shutdown

Patterns / screening significance  
- Depressive cluster: low mood, anhedonia, guilt, fatigue, crying, insomnia  
- Anxiety cluster: generalized worry, panic attacks, somatic arousal  
- Postpartum context: symptoms began within first weeks after delivery; patient is primary caregiver

Risk factors  
- Moderate–high severity of mood and anxiety symptoms, functionally impairing  
- No current suicidal ideation; patient explicitly denies thoughts of self-harm (“never… I would never want to leave him”)  
- Passive cognitions of inadequacy (“he’d be better off with some other mom”) noted; monitor for escalation

Screening impression  
Findings are above threshold concerning for a major postpartum depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; immediate referral for comprehensive clinical assessment recommended. Safety plan reviewed; no imminent self-harm identified at present.
